editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Roger Hal McKain. Mr. McKain served in the U.S. Army with the 8th Air Force. He served in the European Theater, and his highest rank was corporal. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at my home in Mentor, Ohio on February 18, 2005. Roger was 82 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Willoughby, Ohio. Born and raised.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How old were you in 1941?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Um, just a minute here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me the year you were born. I'll do the math.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: '22, but it was December of '22, so you know, you're almost a full year -- you've got a jump.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So was your birthday after December 7 or before?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: 19th.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: December 19. So you were still 18 years old --

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Correct.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: That's correct. Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What are your memories of that day?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Well, we were on a -- my uncle and my aunt and my mother and my grandmother and myself were on our way to Geneva, I believe, to visit my sister and her new husband, relatively new husband. And we heard it on the radio. And I don't recall any great impact that it had on me. I mean, you know, there was some bombing done of our people, but it didn't really -- it didn't shock me or -- I'm not -- I'm eas -- I'm not easily shocked anyway. It didn't shock me. I just -- you know, I figured that's not good. We went on about our activities. There was no conversation, not that I recall. Went to visit and had our afternoon together, and that was it. In January, I believe, the following January or February, I went down to Cleveland to the Air Corps recruiting -- it was Air Corps then --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: -- recruiting station. And my eyes weren't good enough. And that angered me. I had visions of taking movies, look -- watching the bombs go down, you know, and that sort of thing. And they wouldn't take me. And that kind of angered me little. So I said, "All right. You want me; you've got to come and get me." Well, it was March of '43 before I was finally called in. Went in in March. 1st, 2nd, 3rd, somewhere along in there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you work in the meantime? You had a job in the meantime?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: I had a job. Yeah. I was working at the Ohio Rubber Co. Well, I wasn't working when -- in '41. In -- by '43, I was working at the Ohio Rubber Company in their photostat department. And I left there, I think in September of '42 because I knew I'd be called. I wanted a little time, you know, away from work and all. And then I actually entered the service in March of '43.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything in that -- the year or so before you were called for the war effort, getting involved in scrap drives, anything like that?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: No. I don't recall anything like that. I've lived most of my life letting the world happen to me. (laughter) I try to -- I tried to live by the prime directive on Star Trek: Don't interfere with the native population. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Don't want to alter history. (laughter) So you were called in March of '43?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Well, probably earlier. I went in March of '43.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's when you --

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Whatever the time frame is between that, and went from there, from Willoughby to Camp Perry. I was up there maybe two, three weeks. I didn't -- I don't recall the time frame. I missed a weekend pass by about 20 minutes at that location. Then I trans -- I was sent to -- and this was incidentally Signal Corps I was in. And I was sent to Atlantic City for basic training. Stayed in the Ambassador Hotel, 13th floor. Couldn't use the elevators. And I took my basic training there. We had a lot of testing, and they were trying to put me into radio. And I knew I couldn't succeed in radio because I had been a Boy Scout for five years, a Tenderfoot, and couldn't learn Morse code. Couldn't go on to Second Class Scout. So I was sure I couldn't do any good in radio, and I said I knew everything about photography. Well, probably not in those words, but I knew a lot about photography because I'd done a lot. And I thought I knew everything. And so the guy finally, he says, "Well" -- he got me -- he got me a couple of tests. I took the tests. I passed them. He gave me -- I took the other test. I passed. Then they gave me an oral test, and I passed that. He says, "Well, our photo schools are right now -- closed right now, but I'll -- I'll designate you as -- your MOS is 152. That's a photographer." And as an afterthought, he said, "And you'll -- the officer will tell you he wants a picture, but he won't tell you how he -- he won't tell you how to do it." He was trying to scare me, you know. I didn't realize that then. I had no problem with that. I could do anything, you know. And okay. So he made me 152. That turned out to be a dumb-luck decision because I went from Atlantic City at a Signal Corps to Florida; Tallahassee, Florida; Dale Mabry Air Base. And they didn't have Signal Corps attached. They transferred me into the Air Force. I ended up as a photographer in the Air Force, which is what I had in mind, you know, back just right after the war started. And we had our six months there. Oh, in Atlantic City, I missed a weekend pass -- a three-day pass by about two hours. And in Florida, I missed a two -- a two-week pass, two-week -- what do they call it? When you go home?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, furlough?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Furlough. (laughter) Probably by as much as an hour. I had been in an NCO gas class, learning how to handle gas and prevent gas poisoning, all that stuff. And it lasted a couple days beyond when the rest of the guys left. So I got out of that class, and I went over, and I got all dressed up, ready to go, all packed up, ready to go. I went over to the orderly room, and they filled out the papers. They took them -- sent them over to the adjutant's office. He was gone almost an hour. This didn't sound good. Come back. He says, "Well, they've cancelled all those furloughs, and they're calling all these guys back."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: And we were there then again another month, doing nothing, you know. From there, we went up to New York and ultimately the QUEEN MARY over to England.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What else can you tell me about your training stateside before you went overseas?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Well, we had a standard, normal, close-order drill crap you get all the time. I had an advantage over some of the other boys in that my dad had a -- an extended-order drill Army manual. And I learned extended-order drill, just out of dumb curiosity, you know, just reading the thing. And I was able to do that, so I got a sort of training position. And I moved up to PFC and then moved up to corporal rather quickly. And we had extended-order drill. We had a lot of marches. Oh, and the one thing important in that -- well, they were in Florida. They decided we're going to have amphibious training. We had to go to Silver Lake, which was a small lake, but it was crystal clear. You'd see 60 feet down, you know. And they've got a diving board there. And we've got to go there. We've got to take our fuel pack on -- undone, but on -- go up the ladder, drop off into the water, peel off our pack and, you know, swim out. I said, "I can't swim." "Get up that ladder." "I can't swim." "Get up that ladder." "I can't" -- "Jump." You know. I jumped in. My pack came off as I'm going down. I kept going down. Finally two guys (sound effect) come in. They pulled me out. They took me over and pumped me out a little bit. And they were going to teach -- or the one guy was going to teach me to swim. I was over there probably 45 minutes in this little lagoon. And he finally had me do what they call a jellyfish float. You know, that's where you grab your ankles and -- well, that's useless. I mean, you can't -- your head's underwater. It doesn't help you any. But what it demonstrates is your buoyancy. I sank about 18 inches. He said, "If you're ever in a boat, wear a life preserver." (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter) Because you just don't float?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: That's right. I was -- I'm -- I was too dense. (laughter) Probably solid bone in the head. (laughter) But as an aside, it's not relevant to this, but there was a fellow by the name of John Seitz in Willoughby when I was a youngster, and he was probably in his thirties at the time, but he used to go down to the Mentor Beach, when there was a beach, and he'd go down there and get out there about 100 yards maybe. And he's in water up to here. "Come on out. The water's fine." People start out there, and they get out partway, and (sound effect) they go down. Because he was so buoyant, he had trouble getting purchase in the water to swim. He was just the opposite of me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Anyway, where was I?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kind of training did you do for photography?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Very little. We had a photography school, but I really didn't need it because I had done a lot of photography. Before I was in high school, I was -- I was yearbook editor, photo -- camera editor for the yearbook. And I had photographs in every one of the first three issues. '39, '40 and '41, I had photographs in there. So I had done a lot of photography, and I had worked for probably September through maybe April. I'd say that's -- about six months, I'd worked for a professional home portrait photographer. Did processing for him, developed and printed pictures and stuff like that. So that was -- I don't know the term. Well, it was home portrait. Portraiture work. You'd call it portraiture work. And we also did the school annual for the portraits, so I processed all those. So I'd had a lot of experience. And of course as a kid, when you've done a lot of that stuff, you think you know it all, you know. I was satisfied I knew everything there was to know about photography. But I keep losing myself here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh --

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I'd done -- I'd done a little bit of commercial photography, too. Yeah. Up -- prior to my service.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So I guess we're at the point now where you're heading overseas. When was that when you --

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Went overseas in -- I think we left in September, and we arrived in October overseas.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: '43. And that was in Greenock, Scotland. In fact, we left New York on the QUEEN MARY. I was in the observation deck. Of course, it was all boarded over; you couldn't see anything. It's about five bunks high. And that ship, I understood, could travel at about -- they said knots, but somebody interpreted it at 40 miles an hour. It could outrun submarines and torpedoes if it sensed them. You know, detected them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you weren't escorted probably?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Par -- unescorted.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Unescorted?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. Because they were so fast. And we pulled out. We weren't out very long before they turned south and went clear to Florida and then turned around and headed back up toward England because they had detected some submarines -- oh, no, no, no, no. That wasn't it. They had -- some second lieutenant had left his porthole open. So it was -- a light could be seen on the ship. And so they went south to Florida and then headed back up, changed their course. We got to Greenock, Scotland. And after the war is when I heard they had never fired their weapons in anger. They tested them periodically, but never fired at anything. Greenock, Scotland. We got there. And from there, I went down to some -- what's the point they call it when you go for distribution? Doesn't matter. We went down to some central location. I was there maybe a week, and that was near Bedford, Ohio -- or Bedford, England. And of course I had a couple of passes into town. The first time I got into town, I was there. It was dark. It's like 8:30 at night. It was in October. And I was standing in front of a church, which was -- I'd say the door to the church was just beyond your entrance to the other -- other part of the house there. It wasn't very far away. And of course there was a iron -- wrought iron fence there. I'm standing there, trying to -- what to do. And up at the top of the tower, an air raid siren went off. I've always said I think I jumped 5 feet straight up. (laughter) But of course that was my first introduction to it. And then the second was a few days later. I went to a movie, and I was sitting there, and suddenly the thing -- screen partly blacked out. And it says, "Air Raid Alert." And I mean, my tongue went metallic, and I wondered what to do, but nobody was moving. So -- well, if they're not going, I'm not going. So I sat there. And we watched the movie for a little while, and then it come back on. "Alert" -- you know, "Alert Abort -- Over," or something like that. And that was my second experience with -- with air raids and with war. From there, I went to Honington, England, Fire -- Station 595. It was a Honington air base. And I think it was the 1st Strategic Air Depot or something like that. And at that time, I was there two years. And in those two years, I never had a permanent assignment.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were not assigned to any particular outfit?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: I wasn't assigned to any partic -- well, I was probably in an outfit. I can't tell you what it was, but -- but I was a photographer. And the photo section officer took exception to me for some reason. So he wouldn't pull me into this -- into the system, you know, in his department. So I worked the supply room. I worked the mailroom. I worked -- and the depart -- a lot of the department was -- and I've got to backtrack there a little bit. There probably -- every air base probably had anywhere from 18 to 25 men in their photographic department. All of them were identified as 945, which is a photo lab technician. Some of them had been, you know, professional photographers. They were good long-term photographers, but they had that MOS number. Mine was 152, which was identified in the catalogs as photographer/cameraman, photographer, slash, cameraman. I was out on detached service almost all of those two years. I'd go out for 10 days and then come back. I'd be back in for maybe a week or two and then go out for another 10 days. Every detached service assignment was 10 days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kind of assignments would you do then?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: I went to -- anytime an air base had something in the eyes of the commanding officer was a little unusual, then he'd -- he'd say, "We'd better get a professional in here. Or get a real photographer here." He'd look in there and find there was -- the 152 was the number. And he'd check up on the availability. There was only three of us in England. There were probably 3,000 photographers in the air bases, but there's only three of us with that number. And I didn't find that out until after I got out of the service. But I'd go -- I'd go to a -- there was one air base where a plane had been groun -- bellied in, not seriously, in southern England. They'd gone down there and fixed it up enough and put in a mesh runway and flew it up the base to properly do the job. They pulled in there, parked it, and they had it setting there to be worked on. And there was a little pre-engine warmer running. It's like a little gasoline lawnmower with a ductwork that goes up to the engines to prewarm the engines. It's sitting there running, maybe 100 feet away from plane. Putt, putt, putt, putt, putt, putt. Some master sergeant con -- or master or -- it doesn't matter. A sergeant, who should know -- who was under directives not to do this and should have known better. He was up there mopping the plane off with gasoline. The fumes got down to that thing. (sound effect) And that plane just -- (sound effect) And all you could see when you got through was part of the tail and the engines laying on the ground. And so they -- that was something unusual. That's how I happened to end up there. Another instance, I went, and they were having an officers' dance, party. And of course the officers, a lot of them are getting drunk. Male and female, you know. They didn't want their photographers taking pictures at that party, but they wanted pictures. (laughter) Another one, the commanding officer of that base had tried -- he'd used his own photo department, trying to get a portrait. And he just wasn't real pleased with them. So he went through the same routine, and then he realized he had the right person, you know, by signing for a 152. And I went over there and took portraits of him. Well, I can't believe they were better. There's nothing great about them. But I don't -- I can't believe they were better, but I was -- he was presold, you know. I was an expert. They've got to be good. So that's the type of thing that I covered. Yeah. And I did a lot of what they call PR work for -- taking pictures of men working on an engine, pictures in the control tower. And I may even have a couple of those here, that type of picture.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were these pictures for the archives, or did any of them show up in Yank or Stars and Stripes?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Oh, I can't believe -- no, no. We -- a couple of us, not just me, but a couple other guys who were interested and submitted pictures to Stars and Stripes, but I don't remember their ever showing up. I have one picture that was taken by a civilian newsman, and it went, and it was published in the United States, I understand. But I never saw it. So I don't know about that. No. The nearest I came to -- well, first of all, I've often said that to me -- when I go to sleep, it's like a near-death experience. I sleep through anything. Thunderstorms don't wake me up. And every raid we had, I slept through, with one exception. That's the one that blew me out of bed. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's hear about that that.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: That was in London, and I was in a Red Cross billet, where there was probably maybe 80 or 100 GIs sleeping in that facility there, and there were bunks about four or five high. And a V-2 came in about three blocks away. Enough concussion that it tipped over some of the beds. That woke us up. I don't think anybody was hurt, bruises maybe or something, but nobody, you know, nobody was really hurt. But that's the only air raid (laughter) that ever woke me up. And it did. At that time, it brought up various stories and stuff, and one of the guys was saying -- and of course I don't know if it was true, maybe it was just a (inaudible), but he said that there was this bar where there was some civilians in there and some GIs in there. And they're sitting, having their beer, and a bomb went off, you know, a little ways -- a little ways away. The civilians all dived under the tables. The GIs grabbed their beer. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: And I don't know whether it has anything to do with it, but I know for me and I expect a lot of other guys, when you went in the service, you went overseas, you literally wrote yourself off. You just figured you might never go back. And then you lived your -- as best you could, you know. It wasn't a troublesome thing. It's just a fact of life. And so I was -- it was a believable story, but it may not -- may have been a created one.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: At least one of the reasons for the V-1s and the V-2s was to have a psychological impact.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Oh, well -- well, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did it work? (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. The point is they really -- they really wanted to do damage.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: But they wanted to do damage that couldn't be stopped. I -- I was -- I had experiences with the V-1s. They'd go over, and they were -- they were a little putt, putt, putt, putt engine. Putt, putt, putt, putt, putt. Little irregular. Putt, putt, putt, putt. When the putting stopped, that's when they fell, (sound effect) right down. Probably a little arc, but almost -- they just fell straight down. And there were several times -- I remember going through London on a train one time when there was -- and civilian passengers as well, and we could hear one going over. And everybody's sitting there, waiting for it to quit. (laughter) But I was never where one of those went off. And I was only one time near when a V-2 went off, so it was -- I didn't have any known hazardous experiences while I was in the service.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But did -- when you -- did you ever talk to the guys or the British civilians about those -- especially the V-2s?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't know about them until --

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Well, yeah. We knew of them after they started coming in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I mean as far as when you were attacked --

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Oh, I never had conversations with any --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- didn't hear those things till they exploded, right?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Oh, you couldn't hear it. No. No. It was so fast, that it exploded and then you heard it coming in. I think they -- I think it was 2,000 miles an hour or something is what they -- I understand those things traveled at.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But there was no talk about, you know, "This is pretty scary"?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Well, I suppose there was, but I don't recall it. You know, the British at that time had been -- this is -- that would be in '44, I think. '44 -- '43, '44. '44. It had to be almost -- had to have been --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- buzz bombs started in '44.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think the buzz bombs started in '44.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Yeah. Anyway, in '44, the British had been at war for five years, you know. They had gotten sort of -- yeah. It's just another hazard to live with. And I think the -- my interpretation, the -- the mental outlook of the people, as well as a lot of the troops, is it could happen. And they had -- you had to live that, just expect it. There's no way to duck it. So they had a lot of bomb shelters, but they weren't protection against a real close hit. They were protection against shrapnel from something that hit, you know, a few hundred feet away or a few hundred yards away. And a lot of sleeping in subways and stuff like that. But I wasn't involved. I never had -- never was anyplace that I had to get into a shelter. There were lots of shelters there, but just never -- never was a circumstance when I was at the wrong place at the right time for that to happen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think I know the answer to this question from what you were saying earlier. Did you have any close contact with British civilians?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yeah. My -- my really -- my closest contact with British civilians for most of the time I was in the service was those that worked in the Red Cross club and those that operated antique stores and those that gave tours of castles and other land(?) works. I am not a person that's -- I'm not affected by going someplace -- you know, the Seven Wonders of the World would not impress me. I would go, but I'm not impressed. I think it's -- having read about them, seen pictures of them, it's anticlimactic to go. It does not have -- it doesn't move me. And I didn't get to London and go to any -- you know, St. Paul's and those landmarks they have there for better than a year before I went there. The -- I did a lot of stuff going -- I did a lot of tours and went into a lot of antique stores and bought little bits and parts and pieces of things. But then I met -- I had been sent on a special assignment down to the southern coast. There was eight of us went. They'd call it a flight crew. We were down there because a plane had bellied in, and it was repairable. And we were guarding it because that was -- you had to have special orders to go into the area 10 miles from the Channel. Anything 10 miles or closer, you had to have special orders to get there. So we were down there on special orders. There were no GIs down there. And it was unique because if you went into some town, they always were friendly and -- and having a party or having a dance or something like this. That is -- that is the situation I was in when I met the girl I got engaged to. We were there to guard the plane. We were on 24 off -- 24 on/48 off is what you were. And we went to -- some point -- I usually went on my own because I'm not a drinker. All the guys want to go to the bar, you know, in a pub and drink. So I was usually by myself. Some captain or lieutenant or something says, "You know, the guys are a little upset because you never go out with them." I said -- and he said -- I don't remember the whole conversation, but I said, "Well, okay. I'll give it a try." And we went out. We go to a couple of dances. And of course, they always went to a bar or a pub. That's when I had my first alcoholic beverage. And in the course of that period of time, which was just a few weeks, I had found out that I could handle as much as three light ales. If I had more, I lost count, so I always stopped at three light ales. That's only important for what happened later on. I met a girl, and we went out and went to a movie, and we went and had something to eat. And I think I had two dates with her. And I had never had a date when I was -- before I went in the service. And I was extremely naive. But you know, like all guys, you're curious. And I began exploring a little bit. And I wasn't rebuffed. So I continued exploring. And all of a sudden, she said, "You don't even know where it is." She took my hand, led me to a bomb shelter. And I had my first encounter, protected encounter. And that had quite an impact on me. Plus the fact that I'm out of a culture where, you know, that sort of thing, you sort of have an obligation. And I wanted to get engaged. And I gave her -- I had an emerald ring. I gave her that ring as a token until I could get her a proper ring. And I went back to my facilities, my station. And the next time I saw her, we went out, had something to eat, had a movie. No -- no intimacy. And I went back to my facility. And about that time, I got a letter from her. She said she thought it was not a good decision on such a short know -- she sent back the ring. Well, okay, a little disappointed, but you know, I agreed. And I didn't see her then for a few weeks. I went back down there, and we ran into -- I ran into her. And this time, it was -- it was a Saturday over to Monday, a weekend pass. And Sunday, I had said, "I would like to get engaged." And I said, "I can't -- we can't get to a jeweler now, but I'll give you some money. And you can go in and put a down payment on a ring. And then we'll pick it out when -- pick it up when I get back next time." And that went on maybe two weeks, and she sent me a letter saying she had changed her mind. She'd met a boy named Lance, and she was interested in him. So she was breaking engagement. Unfortunately she couldn't get her money back from the jeweler. And no. Okay. I was disappointed, but you know, it was no big deal as far as the money. That didn't mean anything to me. Sometime later, I was back down there. We got together. She agreed to get engaged and went in and bought a diamond ring for her. And I don't think it was two weeks before she said she didn't want to be engaged anymore. Didn't want to marry me. I was too -- too quiet and not exciting enough. And I loved my mother too much. Well, that was three strikes to me, you know, and you're out. And of course the GI -- the guys in the barracks knew about this, what was going on. At that point, they told me, "Well, you're just as well off because we had our way with her, too." And I believed that. You know, of course, at this point, I was not only upset but angry. I believed that. Long -- try to shorten the story. I went to the judge advocate's office because she'd sent a letter claiming she was pregnant. This was -- excuse me. This was several weeks after that. She sent a letter she was pregnant. She sent a letter also to the chaplain and the commanding officer. I went to the judge advocate's department, and I took the letters in, the letter that she'd broken off the engagement and the letter that she'd sent with the pregnancy notice, and talked to the attorney in there. And he says, "Well," he says, "you can marry her and start paying, you know, your allotment, or you can deny it and Scotland Yard will investigate," because the law over there was if someone makes this charge and they can't prove it, it's extortion. "Okay. I'll let Scotland Yard find out for me." And it wasn't very long before I got a letter withdrawing the accusation. So I thought I wasn't responsible. And I left England ultimately, you know, thinking I wasn't responsible. 1995, 10 years ago, a little less than 10 years ago, I got a letter from a woman in England, thought I might be her biological father. And she knew the name of the -- you know, her mother's name was the girl I'd been engaged to. And based on what I knew or thought I knew, I figured she hasn't a chance in the world of finding her father. I figured what probably had happened -- because I had applied for permission to marry, incidentally, and turned down the first time, but reapplied, and it's a long process. They finally had approved that. Before the commanding officer signed it, she broke the engagement for the third time. So it didn't get processed through. And it was a little -- it was sometime after that, maybe two, three weeks after that, I got a letter she was expecting. The bottom line is -- I'm getting lost in time here. The bottom line is when -- when I had -- when I had denied the responsibility and later I got a letter withdrawing the accusation, to me, that signaled that I was not the father.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: And in 1995 is when I got a letter from this woman in England, thought I might be her father. Well, I didn't think I was, but I knew she -- I figured she had no chance. My thinking was this girl has been out with a number of other guys, and she might have thought -- she might have known who it was, but he might have been married and wouldn't have anything to do with her. Anyway, it didn't matter. That detail wasn't important. In the long run, probably wasn't correct. But we chan -- we exchanged letters. A girl named Juliet. I got a picture of her somewhere. Juliet. We exchanged letters. We formed a good bond of friends. And I wrote back, as I say, friendly letters, but noncommittal. I didn't think I was her father, but I didn't think she had a chance of finding him, so I just -- a friendly letter, let her think she'd succeeded. My wife of course is going ballistic when I sent the first letter. She wanted me to just deny it right off the bat. And so the letters continued for maybe a three-week interval. They went on for a little while. Then the -- the chastisement at home by both my wife and my daughter got to be pretty strong, and my daughter said, well, if there was DNA testing or something, that might be a different thing. My daughter in England agreed to pay half the DNA testing, and we had that done. 99.88. So I knew I was her father. I knew it. I had suspected even before we had the DNA testing, I was probably her father, but I was so locked into 50 years of thinking I hadn't been, that I had trouble with that. But anyway, we got that settled. When the letters first started, I could hear my wife and daughter on the front steps talking, you know. And their main concern was she's going to want money. And as it turns out, she didn't need money. She lived better than we did. But when -- that didn't happen, and then when finally after a little time passed, my wife decided I cheated on her, even though, as I say, it was five years before we -- before I met her. And ultimately, long story is -- this was '95, and in 2001, she divorced me. And my daughter went with her. She lived at home. She went with her out to the West Coast. And so they're out there now. And they took (laughter) -- they took almost every photograph I had. (laughter) They didn't take, to my knowledge, any of my war pictures, so to speak, with the exception of those where I was in the picture. And those disappeared, too. And it now looks like they took the first letters, the first packet of letters for the year 1995 that we exchanged, I exchanged with my daughter. Those are the ones I wanted to bring because after we determined -- after we started writing, I began telling her about my, you know, how -- my experiences in England and following the war and going home. And that was stuff I did want to get into, but I -- it's a little foggy now. I don't probably remember it all. But I had -- I tried to tell her the amusing things that had happened and stuff like that. (coughing)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you want some water?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: No, no. That's --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So as far as -- you just had that one protected encountered with her.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: One protected encounter. And then from then, it wasn't. In fact, she initiated the second experience as well. And from that, I think I sort of took the key, so to speak. And -- and the strange part, we were only -- we were only associated for about eight months, and I think -- I don't think we had more than ten encounters in eight months because we didn't have interval -- intimacies each time I went down there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But the other encounters were unprotected, so -- is that what you're saying that --

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: The first one was protected. The rest were not. The rest were not. And obviously based on the dates, the last time I saw her was the time it took.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was the time that it happened.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Because from that point, the date of my daughter's birth was nine months, give or take a few days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was she pretty excited to find out that she had found her father, though?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Oh, I guess she want -- you know, ecstatic. She called a -- she had found out that her stepfather wasn't her father when she was about 13, and that was a bad time. A bad age to find out that you've been lived in a lie. And she reacted very badly. She was screwing up in school and getting into trouble and stuff like that. But -- and she always wondered about her father. It was 1990 that she found out there was an organization in England called War Babes. A woman who had wanted to find her father and thought she was the only one incidentally, at first. She didn't know there was others.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: And she started looking for him, and she was getting rebuffed by the government thoroughly and bounced around a lot. And she'd lose interest -- not lose interest for a while, just be disenheartened for a little while and not do anything. Somehow or other, she -- something came up. I can't remember now. There is a book called Where Are You, Daddy? or something like that that she produced. And at some point in time -- let me see now. Let me think. She began to -- oh, she did -- yes. She did some story in the paper. Somebody had -- some reporter called her about something or other. Or she called about something or other. And he got a little pushy, you know, about finding what she was up to. And she told him. And he did -- he said he'd like to do a story on it. Oh, it was -- it was when they had the -- the 50th anniversary of the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: That would have been --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: 1995. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: '95 for the end --

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: '95. Yeah. And so she thought well, you know, what's she got to lose. She was trying -- what she was trying to do was -- why she called the guy, she was trying to find out any -- any organization she could contact to see who might be coming because she knew her father's name. She'd found out her father's name, but she didn't have any other information on him. Other than his -- he had been born -- he lived -- born in the same city that Lana Turner was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: And so the reporter got -- in talking to her, got to digging, and he said, "Well, I had like to do a story on this." Well, what did she have to lose? You know. He was going to give her the information if he did the story. So she had him do the story. And her mother went ballistic. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: But she didn't find it. She didn't -- nobody had any registration of him coming over for that celebration, so it was all a lost cause. I'm not going to go through this whole thing; that would take days, but ultimately she got -- found out that the place she thought her father was born, Boise, Idaho, was not Lana Turner's town. It was Williams or something like in Montana. Or in -- yeah. Montana. Idaho. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Yeah. Boise, Idaho. It had to be -- it had to be like Williams in Idaho. Up almost to the Canadian border. Again, to shorten this some, at some point or other, she was in touch with a British journalist, if you will, that was doing some work in California. I don't know how she -- I've forgotten how she came in touch with him, but he was interested in her story. And the long and short of it was she said -- she said, "Would you help me? I have this much information, but I haven't gotten any farther." He said he would do that. And about a week later, he called back and he says well, I found out your father -- where he was born. And in the meantime, she had found out from the library, some -- it suddenly occurred to him, what if the newspaper that she read that said Boise, Idaho was wrong? What if her mother had been wrong? Maybe it wasn't Boise. It turned out it wasn't. Lana Turner was born in some other commu -- Williams. Williams is where she was born. And so that gave her a good jump forward. But the bottom line is she ultimately found her father. That guy called back in less than a week. He said he'd been talking to him on the phone. (laughter) And she had a chance to go see him and all. Anyway, we're getting adrift here, but that's --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. But that's how that other woman found --

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Some of the other story.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- possibility --

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's how your daughter found out (inaudible) right?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Well, yeah. Then she heard, in 1990, this -- the woman found her father, I think in '80, '89 or something like that. In 1990, this thing had ballooned on the woman that was looking and turned into an agen -- organization so to speak. It was called -- the press had labeled it the War Babes. And she had found out in the meantime, there were thousands of births in England that -- people that knew they were GI origin, but didn't know their -- don't know their fathers. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So your daughter got involved in the War Babes?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Yeah. She found about War Babes. And it took her four years, even after that, to locate me. But she did finally locate the person she thought was me and sent a -- a registered letter, required a signature, you know. Certainly a certified letter, which I got. And I read it, and I knew right away that she was misinformed, but she had found the right person.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Okay. That was my first -- first --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Reaction?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: -- view of it. And my wife wanted me to just write it off right away. Send her back, "No. Not interested." I just couldn't -- I couldn't do that. I couldn't do that. I wouldn't do that to anybody.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: I don't have a vindictive bone in my body. And I felt actually, you know, some compassion for her because I knew that this has to be a traumatic --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: -- thing for her. And we exchanged letters, probably as many as a dozen letters, before we had the DNA testing done. The DNA testing was done in December after she found me in July. She wrote the letter in July. And that's when my wife -- in fact, when the -- when the information came in -- give you a little insight into my wife. When that information came in, she says, "I knew it. I knew it. If I had known this 45 years ago, I wouldn't have wasted my life." And that didn't sit well with me because I didn't consider our life wasted. You know, we had a roof over our head and food on the table and gas in the car and heat in the furnace, and we'd raised two decent children. And that's a wasted life. But she was just -- she carried an old black cloud over her head all the time. She was negative in every respect all the time. Complaining not only about me, but the neighbors and just anybody and everybody. She was pretty dark outlook on life. But this -- this just nibbled away and nagged away and nibbled away and nagged away. And some point, I finally agreed -- we went to the pastor of the church three times. He couldn't understand all the irate response here. He thought it was necessary. Not only a good idea, but essential that I continue to communicate. But in the final analysis, because my wife and daughter were so adamant, he says, well, to keep peace in the home, I guess you should start -- stop writing, exchanging letters. Well, my daughter in England had known that there was some irritation in the family. And she had already offered to stop writing for a few weeks to see if that would let them get used to having a new family member. So we stopped writing. And this went on for almost six months. And I was still being chastised every time Oprah or Sally or some (inaudible) do a program on people finding each other that they'd looked for.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: I'd get roared at. "Nobody has the right to look for anybody that isn't looking for them." And that just went on and on and on. And anytime even anything come on about England, that chastisement would fire up. And I got tired of it. And I fell back on an old adage, "If you're going to have the name, you're might as well have the game." And I started writing my daughter again. And then shortly thereafter, I decided to go visit her. And I offer -- I asked my wife to go along. And she didn't want to go. So I went over there. It was eight days over there. Met my daughter, met my grandchildren. We had a great eight days together. And I came back. And we continued the letters. And they were now down -- I was -- I had -- was determined because of the chastisement I was receiving at home, I was determined to maintain contact, and I sent a letter every week. One letter every week. And my daughter over there would respond maybe at a couple week intervals, 10 days to two-week intervals she'd respond with a letter. That's the sort of stuff I wanted to bring in because part of the earlier things I sent to her was this -- a better chronological arrangement of the way things took place in my military service. And so anyway, the bottom line is here --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, the mother wasn't still alive when you visited, was she?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Yes, she was. And she was opposed to her daughter finding me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: She didn't want that. But -- because she told her a little different view of the story. You know, she told her I knew all about her and didn't want anything to do with her. And so she was still alive. And in one letter, just as an example, my daughter in England had almost the same relationship with her mother that I had with my wife. (laughter) She said she's not been easy to be a daughter to. (laughter) Anyway, my train of thought's gone again.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't know if you want to get back to your military career. Did you stay in Great Britain the whole time then?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: No. I was tran -- one of my detached services was over to France in, like, April or May of '45. I went over there to -- the commanding officer over there wanted me to come in there and locate a facility and list the equipment needed to set up a photo lab. (End of CD)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: -- went over there and they did, and that was their -- ordinarily they last for 10 days, but I -- you know, you wait for your orders. And I was there like 15 days, no orders, and I'm just potting around, doing stuff, you know, visiting with people. I met a French family over there, and we got acquainted. And I used to eat at their cafe. Cafe Poulan. (phonetic) And eventually, maybe after almost a month, I got a notice from the, you know, the orderly room to come in. And the guy in there was a staff sergeant. He was in charge of the orderly room. And he says -- he says, "You're a pretty popular guy." He says, "I've been getting wires here, faxes" -- not faxes. What did they call them then?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Telegrams?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Telegrams, yeah. Firing back and forth between the commanding officers. The one demanding my return; the other wanting me transferred and that sort of thing. And I said, "Well, you know" -- He said -- oh, he said something. "You're lucky. You're getting to go back. There's a lot of guys here who would like to go back to England." I says, "Well, it doesn't matter much to me. I like it here one place or another." And I said, I'll be back," just off the top of my shoulder. And I shipped out. I went back to England. I was back there. The photo officer put me on the switchboard in his department. I worked that switchboard for maybe six weeks. Five or six weeks. Got orders to go back to France. Went back to France. They had transferred me. The guy in France had more pull, I guess, than the guy in England. I was transferred over there. I was transferred from the 8th to the 9th Air Force. And they had -- by that -- by that time, they had acquired a trailer, like a house trailer, that was equipped as a photo lab. It was their photo lab. So I was in charge of the photo lab. And no really war-related business to do, but I took -- in fact, the first assignment I had was to help make -- fix stuff up for a dance they were having, Ball Americain. And I have a couple pictures somewhere of that where that -- where it was taken. We were making tickets up on just scraps of paper. Cut out, but you know, just like poster paper or something like that. And they -- they had the information about the ball, when it was, what time and all that stuff. And on the back, they were stamped -- just stamped, "Ball Americain." That was so they couldn't be forged. (laughter) But we had that. And then I'm busy finding things to take pictures of. Nothing -- never had an assignment to take a picture. I was just taking pictures. I had one guy under me. And we just pretty much did as we pleased. I'd take pictures and process them, make prints and stuff like that. We didn't have the camera, though. The photo officer and the public relations officer combined had the camera. And we'd borrow for this and borrow for that. But most of the time, I took pictures on a pinhole camera. I'd made a pinhole camera. And I was working there one day, and a gen -- or a major come knocking on the door. He wanted to come in. He was from the inspecting general's office, checking, you know. That was their job, go around checking everything. And we're talking about this and had a nice conversation. And he says, "Where's your camera?" I said, "Well, we don't have a camera, sir. That's in -- the photo officer has that camera." "Oh, where did these negatives come from?" "Well, that's -- we process them." And then he saw some. He said, "Those weren't taken on a pho -- on that Speed -- on" -- C3, they called the Speed Graphic. I said, "No. That's on a pinhole camera. That's our C5." (laughter) And I brought it out, showed it to him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: And we were having a good friendly conversation, so I figured he had a sense of humor and didn't have a problem with it. That next day, we had our camera. (laughter) (inaudible) -- it over to us. So -- but I was there when the war in Europe ended.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Any celebrations?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. I have pictures of a gendarme, French gendarme, with a little mustache and his hair combed down like this. And they're leading him down the street on a rope. And two or three pictures of that particular incident. And I took a picture of the entire Communist party from Merville, France. They all lined up, squatted down, had their picture taken. That's some of the things I took. I took pictures of course of the family that I'd become acquainted with. There was Rosa and her son Christien, who was born of a British soldier, who was Dun -- evacuated at Dunkirk. And there was her -- what they call Maman, and then there was either a sister or a cousin or something, Celeste, and her husband, Andre, and they actually did most of the work in the café. Ultimately, of course, I was shipped back to England. And I ended up -- not too long after I went back, I ended up attached to a nine -- the 977th MP company as photographer. They were forming what they called a -- a combat MP unit. And they had -- part of their TO now included two mechanics, two radiomen and a photographer. And I was assigned to that. I thought, you know -- when I'm going in, I thought, boy, this is the end of the easy life, because that's -- the MPs are a little more rigid, you know, in the way they perform and all. I went to report to the captain there. And he said, "Well, it's you -- your quarters are" -- he told me where my room was, my billet was. This was previously RAF officers' quarters. They were four-room apartments. There was a -- like a living room, a kitchen, two bedrooms upstairs and a bath. And there were five of us in that facility. The two photographers -- or two re -- mag -- mechanics, the two radiomen and myself. And he said, "You don't have any particular duties here. You can do pretty much what you want, but just read the bulletin board every day." He says, "Anytime there's a -- a rifle range or a lecture, you show up for that." And we're sitting there one day, the five of us, bullshitting in the living room there. And all of a sudden, one of the guys look out, and there's formation. And we hadn't heard anything, you know. We dashed out of there like madmen, you know, trying to -- trying to get out in time. We fell in at the end of the line. Without even looking up, the officer says, "Corporal McKain and" -- the other four guys. "Front and center." I figure we're really going to get nailed, you know. Went over there and rep -- you know, stood in front of him. He says, "You men are considered mech -- technicians and therefore will not be required to drill." Of course we immediately felt 110 daggers coming into our back from the rest of the guys. (laughter) But we didn't have anything to do. We just did, you know, just puttered around. I set up a little section where anybody who wanted to learn how to develop pictures could do that. I don't think I ever had anybody come in and do that. But I did do some -- some of my own printing. And we eventually were accepted by the rest of the group because they realized it wasn't our doing. But they were out there doing close-order drill and -- and parading around and taking training and stuff like that. The only thing that was -- the really best thing about that, the really great thing about being in the MP company, they had their own mess hall. And they had great cooks. I mean great cooks. We had good, good food. The first time I ever had -- last time I ever had corn fritters. Didn't even know what they were. I thought -- when they put it on the plate, I thought it was a piece of fish, you know, breaded fish, like. And I bit into it, and that was good. And then I found out what it was. I've never had any since either, but -- fritters, but -- (laughter) that was good.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: I remember that. And also because the hostilities had ceased in Europe, we were getting lots of oranges and stuff from Spain. We were getting a lot of stuff in. And that's when I manufactured my first orange pop.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: I had -- you know, you can -- they gave you oranges whenever you wanted them. You could get some oranges. I took a couple oranges, and I squeezed the juice out, and I dropped an Alka-Seltzer into it to carbonate it. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Eww. That can't have tasted good. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: It did, as a matter of fact. And I tried it maybe a year ago here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: It didn't taste the same.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter) They've changed the flavor of Alka-Seltzer or something.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: I wouldn't be surprised if they remodified that, but also maybe I was using genetically altered oranges.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That could be. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Because I know one thing, the oranges are not like they used to be. They've made them so they don't spoil as quick. They don't -- they don't lose them to spoilage. They can still sell them. But they're not -- it's like tomatoes. You slice a tomato; it's like slicing a cucumber now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: They're not really tomatoes. Bah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Got peaches, they slice like apples. They're crisp. I can remember when peaches weren't crisp.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: But I've drifted again.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, we're -- I guess we're still talking about you were in the Army of Occupation in France then?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: No. I went to Germany.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In Germany?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: When I went out of England, when I left England -- first of all, the war in Japan ended while I was still in the MP company. And from there, I was transferred to Alconbury, England. And I've got to tell you this, too. I got up to Alconbury, England. And people were shipping all over the place. And some people are going home, back to the States. We shipped up there. We were assigned by mistake to a WAC's area and -- because about half the WACs had been shipped out. And they shipped -- sent us to that area. I say improperly. We occupied one half of the compound, and the WACs, the WACs that were remaining, lived in the other half. And they put our group, our -- some of the MPs from our grou -- group as guards. So there was no fraternization. I don't know how well that worked. I never heard whether there was any interchange, but I have to believe there was. And I don't think that the guys from the same outfit would care. They wouldn't put a stop to it, so -- but -- never anything -- My bunk was Sergeant Marion something or other. Had her tag on it yet. (laughter) But I was there until we shipped to Germany. And when we shipped to Germany, we went through -- I don't remember crossing the Channel. It had to be on a boat, a ship. I don't remember that part of the trip at all. But we got to the -- what they called the -- what they called the cigarette camps. They were collecting points for GIs that were going into the occupation. I was in Camp Top Hat and had no money. We'd missed a payday. And there was not a payday coming up for a while, but that was not -- not terribly important. But some of the guys were dealing with the kids that would come up. They'd bring stuff up, you know, and they were buying stuff from them. We were there until -- it came to -- oh, we missed -- a buddy and of mine and I, we missed a formation. We were in the PX. And we got back, and they'd already had a formation. And it turned out they were go -- we were now shipping on our way to Germany. And we hadn't heard anything other than we've got to get ready, get packed up to go. So we put on our -- we had our fatigues on. And I put on my field jacket, and I put on my overcoat. And I had an Army knapsack. In addition to my Air Force musette bag, I had an Army knapsack and of course my barracks bag. And I had the Army knap -- the Army knapsack on, and I had draped over it two blankets. They were just draped over the crossover web -- webbing. And we come out, and we looked like Ziggy, you know --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: -- the two of us. And the other guys were out there in their Class A uni -- they'd been told that we might stop in Paris. So they had their Class A uniforms on. They were ready to have some fun. And they haw-haw, heehaw-hawed us a lot, you know, but nothing we could do. It was too late. We went from there to the train station. We stood in there. And there's a group of Air Force people, our group, that are in there just sort of milling around in a -- in a group, but not really at attention or anything. There was regular Army over to the right. They were in parade -- not parade rest. What's the -- when you can shift from one foot to another. You go to attention and relax one foot. And if you want to change --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: At ease, I know. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Something like that. I don't know -- anyway, I think there was a term. Anyway, they stayed in place, you know. They were -- they were Army. They were organized. They weren't kids. (laughter) Every time there'd be a train come in, our group would start milling around, trying to see what was going on. And the mil -- the Army just stood there until they were told, you know. This went on probably for four or five hours. We were there waiting for a train. Finally they did announce where such and such a group, you know, your train is on track so-and-so. The guys just started running. You know, not in orderly manner. Just started running, running down there. And of course we didn't move as fast because we had all this equipment, all this extra equipment on. And we got -- we were trailing them. When we got down there, you could see ahead of you, the guys were stoping and looking around, trying to figure out what -- you couldn't tell what was up, but -- got down there. It was boxcars. It was boxcars. Not trains. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: They couldn't believe it. Well, then they finally -- what it was. They started piling into the boxcars. And you'd get about ten guys in there, and they'd stand crowded together in the door like, you know, the place must be full. And finally an officer came along. (laughter) He got us loaded. And our baggage all went into a separate -- a separate -- our barracks bag all went into a separate train. So we started out. The boxcars are, you know, they got this kind of crack, cross -- the boards are open so the air can go through and all, sides and everything. It's just not any resistance to weather. And it's turned night now, and this is November. We're going along, and these guys are stomping around, trying to keep warm and all. And my buddy and I shared the two blankets. We laid the one blanket down, put the other blanket over us -- over us, and had a mess cup with a candle in it in there, just -- our knees propped up. We were as warm as toast. And these guys are going up and down there and stomping on the -- on the floor and everything. And every once in a while, we'd say, "Ho, ho, haw, haw. (laughter) Goin' to Paris."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: (laughter) At some point during the night, they stopped the train, and the officer got the baggage car opened, and they were able to get stuff out so they could get warm and, you know, get some jackets and stuff on, but -- And we never -- we went -- I joked, I joked in writing about it, said we went around Paris five times and never went in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: We did go past Paris. I think we did go around it, you know, one side. But as we got into Germany, we had some fun there by -- we're riding -- it turned out, we found out that there are carriages ahead of us, coaches ahead of us with German -- returning German prisoners of war who had been prisoners, who were on their way back home. And we are in boxcars being pulled through. We had a lot of fun going -- we'd pull into a station. Germans down there. Yeah. Police, these guys. And then we'd come along, and we're waving and everything. And they would look perplexed. Their guys were in carriages. We're in boxcars. (laughter) And we stopped at some station some point, and they had a long trough along a wall, the side of a wall, with faucets. It was like a sink, only it was a long sink. And we got out of there and took off our shirts and stuff and washed up and everything. And it was cold because there were people in there with their overcoats on. (laughter) We had some fun because we knew it was perplexing to them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: (laughter) But -- and we got to Germany, Thanksgiving Eve. Oh, and that brings a point up. I was over in England, over in the service in Europe for two and a half years. And I had K rations Thanksgiving and Christmas every year. Circumstances were such that's what I had. K rations -- C rations. K rations.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No turkey meal or turkey dinner, huh?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: No. No turkey dinner. Never had turkey while I was over there. (laughter) In fact, there was one time -- like I said, I was on a detached service once. It's not uncommon for me to go back after the evening meal had been served. And I don't know what they had that night, but they had -- they had pork chops. And I love pork chops. And I had plenty of pork chops. (laughter) I went back for third and fourths on pork chops, but -- Where are we now? We just got -- we just got into Germany.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Got into Germany. You were -- how long were you in Germany?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Got there Thanksgiving night and left the last -- the last of January, earliest, first of February. I forget that date. I may even have that in one of these papers here. Oh, I don't think so. Anyway, but something occurred to me that was of interest there. Oh, I got to Germany. Came in casual. And we were sent to Erbenheim Aerodrome, former Air For -- German Luftwaffe base. Had a lot of damage. And come in there and got our billet. We reported. Got in line to be assigned to do something. And we're going up through this stairway and hallway, up to the -- to finally go into the office there. Most of the guys were being assigned to detail, you know, to go out and help clean up the place. I come around the corner there. And I stood in front of this officer. He's lieutenant. He looked up. And it's the staff sergeant from that instance back when I left France in -- earlier in '45. He looked up, and he says -- he got up and he stuck out his hands. We shook hands. He says -- (coughing) (inaudible) -- when he made that move, that was a little maybe -- his captain there that was nearby might think it was strange. He looked right, he says, "Captain, I'd like you to meet (inaudible) McKain. Very much in demand in the UK." (laughter) And he fumbled around, looking through some papers, and he finally says, "Would you want to go to public relations school?" "Sure." So I went to public relations school in Wiesbaden and -- instead of bringing in hunks of steel and hunks of concrete. (laughter) I lucked out. Another dumb-luck thing that happened. I completed my time in Wiesbaden after a period of some -- you know, a few days. And I'm out near a bus stop to go back to the air base, and the officer comes along in a Jeep, Warrant Officer Texel (phonetic). He had been the officer in charge of our group in Alconbury. And he recognized me. He stopped. He says, "You need a ride?" I said, "Yeah. I'm going to the base." He said, "Where you working?" I said, "Well, I don't really have a job yet." He says, "Well, you can come in our photo department." (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: So I ended up in the photo department at Erbenheim Aerodrome. And again, the war was over, so you know, the most official job I had in the -- let's see. That would have been -- God. I've kind of lost track. I know I've got some letters that would give me the details. That had to be late '45.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Late '45, early '46.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Yeah. And the only official job I had there was we had to print up a bunch of 8x10s that was a montage of an air base and some 17s flying over. They'd been combined into one picture. And we had to make those up. And they were for some general to send home as Christmas cards. (laughter) That's the nearest thing I had to an official job. The rest of the time, I was taking pictures. We had -- there's three of us assigned there. We had about five cameras. So we had a camera anytime we wanted it and plenty of film. And I took a lot of pictures of the Red Cross girls. I took pictures of some of the sites around Germany, around Wiesbaden. Just filling time. Just filling time. Another experience I had there was I did want -- I was not interested in a lot of the souvenirs, but I would have liked to have gotten a nice pair of binoculars. Finally found out there was some guy in some abode, some building where people live, apartment building like. He had a -- some binoculars he wanted to sell. I had probably -- because I don't smoke, I had probably eight cartons of cigarettes. And cigarettes were extremely valuable over there. I went down there prepared, you know, to deal. I'd have given him all eight for the binoculars. Got there and all he wanted was coffee. He didn't want anything but coffee. And I could have got him coffee because a buddy of mine was a staff -- was the sergeant in the mess hall, and they had coffee. But I also knew that there'd been a late shipment hadn't come, and they were low on coffee. They had it, but they were low on coffee. And I wasn't going to take the coffee away from the guys that liked it. I don't like coffee, so I wouldn't miss it, but I wasn't going to take it away from the rest of guys just to get my binoculars, so I didn't get the binoculars. But I'm trying to think if there was anything else. Nothing related to that. The -- one other incident occurs to me there. A fellow, another GI, had gone -- the guys were going to -- on furloughs, if you will, to Switzerland. And he went to Switzerland and came back with about five watches. And the watch I bought for him -- from him, I gave him a carton and a half of cigarettes for it. That was a dollar and a half cost to me, and he gave me the watch that he'd gotten for a GI raincoat. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: And so I had a nice watch. I later learned that he sold them to a guy at $80 a carton, who was going to Berlin where he could get $150 a carton.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: After I got out of service, two or three years, I read a little blurb in the Reader's Digest where they wondered whatever happened to all those cigarettes because they found in tracking, checking in all, that cigarettes would be bought on the black market in Berlin or anyplace. And whoever bought them, if it was a city dweller, they'd take them out to the country and exchange them for meat. They couldn't get meat real easy. The farmer out there was raising meat, would take them in and exchange them for tractor parts and stuff. They wondered if any of them ever got smoked (laughter) because they were -- they were currency.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: And valuable currency.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It didn't matter how old they got.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: That's right. If they're unopened. They probably had some value opened even, but you know -- because I used to use them to get haircuts and for tips and get laundry done, that sort of thing, is where I used most of my cigarettes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Like I say, I'm not a smoker. The nearest I came to smoking was going way back to England. When I was first over there, I used to go, like, to the corner exchange or something where they're having a dance. I don't dance, but it was someplace to go. I'd stand around visiting with other GIs and with the girls that were British military. They were Land Army. They had a lot of different female organizations for various jobs. And I'd hand out cigarettes. You know, I'd pass out cigarettes. And I would stand there with a cigarette lit, but I didn't really smoke it. I was just -- something to do with my hand. I can't stand tobacco smoke. (laughter) From the time I was 4 years old, I had a problem with tobacco smoke, but that was -- let's see. That was -- that -- My train of thought there was back in Germany, and when I -- I bought a -- an Iron Cross from some kid, probably 8, 10, 12 years old, somewhere along in there, for a pack of cigarettes, which I'm sure was turned to some other purpose. I don't think he smoked them. Might have, but I don't think so. He probably was -- because they're valuable. He took them and used them in trade.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So then you probably finally came home, right?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Final what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Finally came home, right?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. We finally left Germany. And I missed -- I almost missed that trip, too. I only missed a couple of gatherings or fallouts or whatever you have. I overslept a little bit, and all the guys were out there. And of course, they were -- you could hear they were getting ready, getting loaded on the trucks. And I jammed all my stuff in my barracks bag, and I rushed out of there and got to a truck just before they were ready to close the gate. Or I'd have probably been there another week or two. Probably gone out on the next shipment or something, I suppose, but -- Then we took -- it was a hospital train that we were taking from Germany up to Antwerp, Belgium. And of course they had beds. They were stacked a little bit, two or three high, but there was beds. And I stayed in that bed. We had C rations instead of K rations, and I stayed in that bed the whole trip. Never had -- well, I got out and went to the john and stuff, but I just stayed there. Well, there were no seats either for that matter, but -- And I don't think it took terribly long. It might have been a little over a day. I forget now. But we loaded -- I went over on the QUEEN MARY and came back on a Liberty ship. Oh, and there was an amusing incident related to that then. Coming back, it's -- it was probably about 10 days. Come back across on a Liberty ship. And they had their mess hall -- I'm sure almost all the ships were the same way. They have a table about this long, maybe a little longer and a little narrower, but there was a rib all the way around because that kept the stuff from sliding off as the ship, you know, rocked and rolled. One morning we're in there for breakfast, and we're sitting there eating, and the ship rolled over a little bit, and all the trays slid down one. And they -- now you've got another guy's tray in front of you. One guy threw up into the tray. Then they slid back. That guy threw up when he got it back. And the rest of us got up and left the table. (laughter) I never got sick, but (laughter) that was a memorable occasion.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: And that reminds me back to the QUEEN MARY. There were guys sleeping on the deck. There were 17,000 troops on that QUEEN MARY, plus a crew of 1900. And guys were sleeping on the decks, literally sleeping on the decks instead of in -- inside anyplace. I don't remember any memorable meals there. I do remember one meal I didn't eat was -- what's that? It's sheep or goat or something. Haggis --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Lamb?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Haggis, they call it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, haggis. That's lamb stomach or something.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Something like that. Yeah. I didn't eat that. But I -- it was no problem. Oh, and what I was going to -- what I was leading up to here is of course we'd go out on deck occasionally, and the -- and the front of the ship had a good-sized deck. Probably was enough room for eight or nine hundred guys out there, and they're out there just, you know, enjoying what they're seeing and taking in the breeze and all. I don't smoke, but I was the only one that could light a cigarette on that deck. In New York, I spent one -- we had a 12-hour pass. I spent maybe six hours in New York on that 12-hour pass from Camp Kilmer in New Jersey, where we were embarking from. And I had bought a cigarette lighter that was just like any other cigarette lighter except that out of the bottom, there was a long cord -- it was probably about 24 inches long -- of some composed material. When you -- when you hit the -- hit the flint, that would glow. And the harder the wind blew, the hotter it got, you know. It was a -- some kind of material that was incendiary, but not inflammable. It never turned into a blaze. And I lit a lot of cigarettes (laughter) on that -- on that deck going over.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you probably finally got home in the spring of '46 sometime?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: I got home in March of -- I was in the service three years and four days. I got home in the early part of March, and I come out of Indiantown Gap. And that was an efficient operation. We were there 24 hours, and we were moving most of that time because they -- they had -- you'd go to this thing for this thing, go to that thing, go to this thing, make (inaudible), eat. You go someplace else. A lot of processing. And very efficiently done. And one -- the only -- nearest thing to a hitch was -- was no hitch at all. As the guy was processing me and he said -- I said something about being in the armed forces. What he got to hear is the armed services -- the armored services. He had AA instead of AF. I said, "Will that -- will that slow my discharge?" "No." "Forget it." (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: And took the train and stopped to visit a girl that I had corresponded with in -- God. Near Esbyville/ S'B'ville(?), Pennsylvania. I can't remember the name of the town. And then I stayed with her folks there. I stayed overnight. And we went out to a movie and dinner. And then I came on home, came into Cleveland. And my brother-in-law picked me up, took me home. Trying to think if there's anything else relative to that. Something popped in and popped out real fast.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Well, it may come to me. May come to me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. Well, I'll tell you what we'll do here -- (Break in audio)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: We were there. We're all green soldiers. And you know, new enlistees and stuff. We're out on a field trip. Spend the night in the jungles there in Florida. At night, it was dark -- I mean, it was black. We had to do guard duty. We had live ammunition. (inaudible) just intermittently(?). That's no problem there for the moment, but it was an element of risk because you've got green people, a lot of them never had a weapon or anything before. And you had to challenge anybody that came along. And there was a remote, but possible of somebody getting hurt, chance of it. But you know, we got through that all right. I'll jump forward now to the time I was on that special assignment in southern England where we were guarding an aircraft that had bellied in. We were out there. This is an area where there was concern about paratroopers dropping in, you know, stuff like that. They wouldn't give us any ammunition because some of the guys were shooting at jackrabbits.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: (laughter)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Great. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: And this is a Red Cross girl, Adelaide Field(?). That Christmas tree is made up of -- there are three real -- it's a real Christmas tree. That's in Germany. Wiesbaden. We had three real decorations on it, but the rest of them are ping pong balls dipped in paint and rolled in Epsom salts. And the tinsel is -- the foil that they wrapped --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right, right. Whatever they called that.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Same -- same girl.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
