sp.p: -- per Cubs. They weren't Piper Cubs, but they were -- I think it was a C-46 or something like -- little cargo. Hold about six, eight people, I guess. Each -- independently fly or riding in an aircraft and taking oblique views of battle damage from about 1500 feet over Germany and France and Belgium, that sort of thing. And that's the nearest thing I came to being involved in aer -- aerial photography. I did work in the one laboratory for a while, a very short length of time, with processing negatives from -- they were mapping, aerial mapping, all of Europe. And they were shooting at like maybe 2,000 feet or something. I forget the exact altitude. And I was involved in some of the processing of that, not the taking of the pictures. And then for a very short length, like two or three days, I worked in a laboratory where they were making dye transfer prints. And that's excellent color, but it's a complex process. I don't suppose anybody does that anymore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: There's better ways to do it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- those pictures still hold up?

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: I don't know how well they would hold up. I know that the early color photographs that became -- that came out of the civilian market, were not good quality. They didn't have much life expectancy. And for quite a few years, the color was not of great quality. It was -- it was good. It was colorful, but the life, the lifespan was shortened.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: The only way you could prolong it was to keep them, you know, confined inside of a book, put in a drawer or something like that, where they didn't have exposure to light. I have a few color pictures that came from various family members that are still pretty good, but they've always been, you know, in an album or in a drawer or a box or something. I've also had a lot of them that were just generally circulated, and they fade away pretty fast.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: They do seem better now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've had some that were from 40 years ago that -- that were put away, and they still faded. (laughter)

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Right. Yes. Right. Yes. Exactly. Yeah. And of course sometimes that's the processing. The same in reverse. Most of my work has been black-and-white photography. I worked for a newspaper for four years after -- well, after I was out of the service. And I processed all my own pictures. I've got pictures that were processed -- I used to process newspaper standards. That meant they were only probably washed about five minutes instead of an hour. And they could stain and fade. I've got pictures that haven't stained and faded. But I wasn't always diligent about rushing them through. And so some of those may have been washed the proper amount of times. You have to wash the fixing agent out of them. That's what causes them to stain.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: But I've shied away from color photographer for a long time because I wanted to do my own processing and I couldn't afford the necessary equipment and situation --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: -- that could accommodate that, so I just never really got into that. The last 15, 20 years here maybe, sometime since I retired, I began taking a lot of color film, getting color prints and putting them away. And that's about the best you can do with them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: But one thing, I think -- I haven't been able to test this. It's been too recent. They now have good color reproduction by xerox.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: And those -- I've got a lot of those pictures exposed to where they're getting daylight on them from incandescent and regular daylight. They're getting light on them all the time, and they don't seem to be changing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: So that may be one way. Because those are not a photographic image. Those are inks --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: -- that have been picked up and transferred. Of course, ink can last a long time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I've been able to fix up some pictures --

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Pardon.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've been able to fix up and make some pictures by -- just by doing that.

sp.speaker: Roger Hal McKain
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. (End of Interview)
